Moving to the smaller tidystata core

Source: MIGRATION.md

tidystata 0.3.0 is a breaking release focused on data exploration and preparation. Four wrappers have been retired: read_data(), write_data(), esttab(), and codebook_detail().

These functions are no longer part of tidystata and are unsupported; the sections below name the packages to use instead. The retained exploration and preparation helpers remain available. The upstream comparison below also records earlier retirements.

This file is the authoritative migration guide in the source repository. The same guide is published as the website’s Migration guide article. Code blocks are recipes to run deliberately; examples that read or write files require your own paths and any named optional packages.

To try local changes, open the source project and restart R, run devtools::install(".", upgrade = "never", build_vignettes = FALSE), then restart R again. After library(tidystata), inspect packageVersion("tidystata") and find.package("tidystata"). Opening a repository does not itself replace an older installed package.

Changes from the GitHub 0.2.0 baseline

Compared with upstream commit 12709f6, 54 exported objects become 46: 11 exports are removed, while timer(), preview_table(), and unpreview_table() are added. This comparison includes local changes made before the four-wrapper milestone and the restored printing/slicing helpers.

Previous upstream exports Current destination or replacement
s_time() Renamed to timer(); timing messages use compact duration text.
cut_quantile() Now xtile(), the Stata command it follows; cut_quantile() stays as a quiet alias.
s_match() Renamed to varlist(), since it parses a Stata varlist string; the old name works with a deprecation warning.
s_try() Now capture(), after Stata’s capture; s_try() stays as a quiet alias.
names_as_column() Now ds(.type = "table"); names_as_column() and ds_as_column() stay as quiet aliases.
tab2(), fre2() Kept as the cross-tabulation functions; tab2() with three or more variables now returns every pairwise table, as Stata’s tab2 does.
read_data(), write_data() Retired; use format-specific packages directly.
codebook_detail() Retired; use codebook() or datawizard::data_codebook().
tidy_coef() Reworked locally as esttab(), then retired; use broom/broom.mixed directly. esttab() was not an export in this upstream revision.
regress(), regress_data(), regress_coef(), regress_stat() Retired; fit models and extract results directly.
s_plot(), s_ggsave() Retired; use ggplot2 functions directly.
print_headtail(), print_interval(), slice_headtail(), slice_interval() Restored as reviewed active functions; original tracked implementations remain in Git history. Use preview_table() for a persistent display style that retains every row.

The original printing classes and their S3 registrations remain retired. The new tidystata_preview class operates on full tables; it does not pretend that a row subset contains the full data. Retired implementations are unsupported and are not distributed in the package. The restored printing and slicing helpers were reworked and may differ from their 0.2.0 versions.

The package itself is renamed from statart to tidystata: replace library(statart) and statart:: with library(tidystata) and tidystata::. The bundled starwars dataset is removed; use dplyr::starwars (dplyr 1.1.4 or later). lifeexp keeps its columns and labels but is rebuilt from World Bank World Development Indicators, so its values differ slightly from Stata’s lifeexp.dta.

Renamed arguments

Argument names now follow one rule: options after a ... that takes columns or expressions are dotted, and functions without ... use plain names (see CONTRIBUTING). The old names still work with a lifecycle deprecation warning.

Old call New call
destring(.x), decode(.x), var_type(.x, .abbr), var_unit(.x) x, abbr
na_if_value(.x, .value), value_if_na(.x, .value) x, value
timer(.x, .on_error), capture(.fn), set_seed(.fn) x, on_error
s_merge(.keep, .assert, .generate, .report) keep, assert, generate, report
varlist(ignore.case) ignore_case
summ(.na.rm = TRUE), tabstat(.na.rm = TRUE) .missing = FALSE
summ(.mode), tabstat(.mode) .type (same values)

Enumerated options such as .type, .wt_type and method must now be spelled out in full: rlang::arg_match() rejects abbreviations that match.arg() accepted, and suggests the intended value. tab2() and fre2() gain .by, which returns one cross-table per group in a named list.

Stata names and aliases

Several functions now carry their Stata names. The earlier names still work as quiet aliases, with no notice, and are documented on the same help pages.

Stata Function Aliases
tab2 x y tab2(); fre2() adds totals xtab()
mvdecode x, mv(-98 -99) mvdecode(x, c(-98, -99)) na_if_value()
mvencode x, mv(0) mvencode(x, 0) value_if_na()
destring destring() as_numeric()
decode decode() as_character()
tostring tostring() (new: codes as text, ignoring value labels)
egen pc() pc() pct()
egen tag() is_first() s_tag()
egen rownvals() (egenmore) row_nvals() (new: ignores missing values unless .missing = TRUE)
tab x, gen(x_) as_dummy() tab_gen()
xtile xtile() cut_quantile()
capture capture() s_try()
ds ds(); ds(.type = "table") for a table ds_as_column(), names_as_column()
list s_print() (new: style = "headtail", "interval" or "all")
set seed 123 set_seed(123), now also alone; the pipe form x |> set_seed(123) is unchanged

var_type() and var_unit() are now the primary names; s_type() and s_unit() still work but are deprecated with a lifecycle warning. pct() shares its name with gt::pct(), so prefer pc() when gt is attached.

One behaviour changed: several codes in na_if_value(x, c(-98, -99)) now mean “any of these”, as in Stata, instead of an elementwise comparison as in dplyr::na_if(). A single code works as before.

tidystata does not define search(), describe() or lookfor(), which would mask base R, Hmisc/psych and labelled. Use findit(), variables() and variables_search().

Weights

Stata’s weight clauses map to .wt and .wt_type:

Stata tidystata
tab x [fw = w] tab(d, x, .wt = w)
tab x [aw = w] tab(d, x, .wt = w, .wt_type = "analytic")
tab x y [fw = w] tab2(d, x, y, .wt = w)
summarize x [aw = w] summ(d, x, .wt = w, .wt_type = "analytic")
xtile q = x [aw = w], n(5) mutate(d, q = xtile(x, 5, wt = w))

Frequency weights may be non-integer, unlike Stata’s [fw], matching dplyr::count(wt =). For survey designs that need design-based standard errors, use srvyr or survey; tidystata’s weighted standard errors treat the weights as frequency or analytic weights only.

Correlations, missing values and chi-square

Stata tidystata
pwcorr x y z, sig obs pwcorr(d, x, y, z)
pwcorr x y z (matrix) pwcorr(d, x, y, z, .wide = TRUE)
spearman x y pwcorr(d, x, y, .method = "spearman")
misstable summarize misstable(d)
misstable patterns misstable(d, .patterns = TRUE)
tab x y, chi2 V tab2(d, x, y, .chi2 = TRUE)

pwcorr() uses pairwise deletion as Stata does; drop incomplete rows first for correlate’s listwise deletion. misstable() treats empty strings as observed, unlike Stata; convert them with mvdecode() first.

Standardising, percentages and dummies

Stata tidystata
egen z = std(x) mutate(d, z = std(x))
by g: egen z = std(x) mutate(d, z = std(x), .by = g)
egen p = pc(x) mutate(d, p = pc(x))
tab x, gen(x_) as_dummy(d, x, .names = "index")

as_dummy() names columns by category (x_male) unless .names = "index". For model formulas, factors already expand to dummies.

Panel lags and leads

Stata tidystata
xtset id year then gen l = L.x mutate(d, l = s_lag(x, time = year), .by = id)
L2.x, F.x, D.x, D2.x s_lag(x, 2, ...), s_lead(x, ...), s_diff(x, ...), s_diff(x, 2, ...)
xtset id year, delta(5) s_lag(x, time = year, delta = 5)
xtset id month (%tm) s_lag(x, time = date, unit = "month")
xtset id t with %tc clock times s_lag(x, time = datetime, unit = "hour")

There is no xtset state to declare: give time = in each call and the panel with .by. Unlike dplyr::lag(), which shifts rows, gaps in time give missing values. Time values must be unique within each panel. Numbers (including Stata %tm/%tq variables read by haven), dates, date-times, tsibble or zoo period classes and ordered factors (such as survey waves) all work as time; text and unordered factors must be converted first.

Assertions, tags and listings

Stata tidystata
assert x > 0 assert(d, x > 0)
by g: assert _N == 1 assert(d, n() == 1, .by = g)
egen t = tag(id) mutate(d, t = is_first(id))
list print_all(d)

assert() counts a missing result as a contradiction, while Stata treats a missing value as larger than any number; write is.na(x) | x > 0 for Stata’s behaviour. is_first() returns TRUE/FALSE rather than 1/0.

Coming from Stata: where to find the rest

tidystata covers the everyday Stata data loop: inspecting, selecting, tabulating, summarising, preparing and checking. For other Stata commands, these packages are the recommended R tools:

Stata R
regress, reghdfe, esttab/outreg2 fixest, modelsummary
reshape tidyr::pivot_longer(), tidyr::pivot_wider()
winsor2 datawizard::winsorize()
binscatter binsreg (or statar::stat_binmean())
tsset monthly/quarterly periods tsibble (yearmonth(), yearquarter())
svyset, svy: srvyr, survey
use, save, import haven, readr, readxl

statar can be attached alongside tidystata. Only tab() and xtile() share names; attach tidystata last, or call tidystata::tab(). statar’s tlag()/tlead() correspond to tidystata’s s_lag()/s_lead().

findit() looks up the R equivalent of a Stata command from the console, such as findit(reg) or findit("merge 1:1 id, keep(match)"); Stata’s abbreviations work, and findit() alone lists every entry. The website’s “Coming from Stata” articles, in English and Chinese, show the same list by topic with notes.

Import and export directly

Choose the package for the format you use. Install only that package and its dependencies. For example:

survey <- readr::read_csv("survey.csv")
readr::write_csv(survey, "survey-clean.csv")

survey <- haven::read_dta("survey.dta")
haven::write_dta(survey, "survey-clean.dta")

survey <- readxl::read_excel("survey.xlsx", sheet = 1)
openxlsx::write.xlsx(survey, "survey-clean.xlsx")

saveRDS(survey, "survey.rds")
survey <- readRDS("survey.rds")

Other direct alternatives include haven::read_sav()/haven::write_sav() for SPSS, haven::read_sas() for SAS datasets, haven::write_xpt() for SAS transport files, arrow::read_feather()/arrow::write_feather() for Feather, and jsonlite::fromJSON()/jsonlite::write_json() for JSON. SAS transport output uses an .xpt extension; it is not a .sas7bdat file.

Extract model results directly

Use broom for coefficient and model summaries:

fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
broom::tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
broom::glance(fit)

For supported mixed models, use broom.mixed::tidy() and broom.mixed::glance(). These return numeric results for subsequent formatting; they do not reproduce the retired wrapper’s combined coefficient strings or significance stars.

Detailed codebooks

Use tidystata::codebook() for the retained compact variable overview. For the previous detailed codebook capability, call the underlying package directly:

datawizard::data_codebook(mtcars)

Table return types

Table-producing helpers now preserve the input container by default: base data.frame inputs return base data.frames, tibbles return tibbles, and data.table inputs return data.tables. This applies to frequency tables, summ()/tabstat(), codebook(), variable inventories, and name tables, including empty results. Existing list outputs remain lists, with each table using the input container. If downstream code requires a tibble regardless of input, convert explicitly with tibble::as_tibble().

New summaries and inventories are ungrouped. Grouping columns still appear where the function normally reports them; selection and slicing retain valid grouping. New data.table summaries do not inherit keys or indexes from the input. Arbitrary subclass metadata is not copied onto newly shaped tables. Vector and scalar helpers retain their existing return shapes, and statistical conventions are unchanged.

Frequency-table output

fre() and fre2() default to .type = "auto", preserving the input container. fre1() returns a list of tables in that container, like tab1(). Explicit .type = "tibble" requests a tibble, including in tab1() and fre1(). To request rich formatting, install flextable and specify the type:

tidystata::fre(mtcars, cyl)
tidystata::fre1(mtcars, cyl, gear)
tidystata::fre(mtcars, cyl, .type = "tibble")
tidystata::fre(mtcars, cyl, .type = "flextable")

The default return type is independent of whether flextable is installed. Requesting rich output without it installed produces an installation message.

For tab(), tab1(), fre() and fre1(), an explicit .by replaces existing group_by() groups; the default NULL inherits them. Percentages percent and cum use all observations within each group and range from zero to 100. valid and valid_cum exclude observations with missing measured values, while retaining missing grouping keys as ordinary groups. Cumulative percentages follow displayed order.

Frequency tables append total rows. With up to five measured columns, the final measured column becomes character to hold total labels; wider joint tables use a separate label column. Value labels for distinct original values can look identical, and observed categories can match total labels. Use tab() or tab1() when original category values and types are needed. The final row of fre2() is the marginal total even if an observed row category is also "total".

decode() uses value labels only when the labelled vector has a nonempty labels attribute. Vectors without value labels use ordinary character conversion, including tagged missing values.

One-way tabulation accepts list columns and counts their distinct values. Matrix columns are unsupported. Selecting no variables returns an empty result: tab1() and fre1() return empty lists by default, while table output has zero rows. tab2() and fre2() return an empty table for a zero-column selection; other selections must contain exactly two variables.

Persistent previews and explicit row subsets

Use preview_table() when a long table needs a compact console display while all rows remain available to subsequent research steps:

prepared <- survey |>
  dplyr::arrange(respondent_id) |>
  tidystata::preview_table(style = "headtail", n = 10) |>
  dplyr::mutate(income_log = log(income))

prepared # Prints selected rows; calculations still use the complete table.

The wrapper adds class tidystata_preview to the full table, preserving its underlying data.frame, tibble, or data.table container and supported grouped and rowwise metadata. Printing uses a temporary tibble. Its style persists through supported selection, filtering, arrangement, mutation, grouping, summaries/reframing, and pivots. Joins inherit the left table’s settings; bind_rows() inherits the first input’s settings. External dplyr and tidyr verbs follow their own container and grouping rules; for example, dplyr::group_by() creates a grouped tibble. Other containers and lazy tables require explicit conversion or collection first. tidystata table-producing helpers carry supported preview settings to their results, including tables inside list outputs.

style = "headtail" displays the first ceiling(n / 2) and final floor(n / 2) rows. style = "interval" displays approximately evenly spaced row positions, including both ends when n >= 2. Sort the table first when these positions should cover a meaningful order. n is a total row budget, not a count for each end: it must be a positive integer or Inf. A budget of one selects the first row. If the table has at most n rows, every row appears once; larger budgets never duplicate rows. Row positions refer to the entire current table, including grouped tables, rather than sampling within each group.

survey |>
  dplyr::arrange(income) |>
  tidystata::preview_table(style = "interval", n = 6)

ordinary <- tidystata::unpreview_table(prepared)
# tibble::as_tibble(prepared) and as.data.frame(prepared) also remove the preview.

unpreview_table() removes only the preview behavior, leaving all rows, the underlying container, and supported grouping intact. Wrapping and unwrapping data.tables copy them before modifying preview metadata; later explicit native data.table mutations retain normal reference semantics. Explicit as_tibble() and as.data.frame() conversions choose the requested container and remove the preview. Ordinary tibble printing may still truncate its console output according to tibble options.

For a single display, use print_headtail() or print_interval() with the legacy argument names. They print selected rows and return the original input invisibly, so a pipeline continues with the complete data. To intentionally reduce the data, use slice_headtail() or slice_interval(); these return real subsets in the input container. Previews and row subsets preserve base data-frame row names. All four helpers use the same total-n selection rules above. They replace the archived implementation’s duplicate-row and odd-budget behavior.

Variable names and metadata

ds() returns a character vector of selected names. ds_as_column() and names_as_column() are equivalent and return a one-column table named name in the input container. Use tidyselect in ... to select or rename existing columns; it does not create computed columns. Selection on grouped data retains grouping keys, following dplyr::select(); ungroup first when these keys should not be included.

variables() returns a name column and adds label only when at least one selected variable has a usable label attribute. Other labels are then NA. It reads variable attributes, not value-label mappings. Selection and renaming retain these attributes, and the input is not modified.

variables_search() searches names and variable labels, not cell values. Pass one non-missing character string; vectors, NA and non-character queries now produce a clear error. An empty query matches all selected variables. Matching is case-insensitive and searches substrings by default. Use ^age$ for a complete name or label, and *, ? or ~ for zero or more, exactly one, or one or more characters. One range such as [a-h] or [1-12] is supported. Numeric ranges expand into alternatives; use unanchored patterns such as item[1-12] for substring matching. Multiple ranges and arbitrary regular expressions are outside the supported pattern language.

Compact inventories and browsing

codebook() returns one row per selected variable for the complete input, including grouped inputs. It ungroups before selection, so grouping keys are included only if selected or if all columns are requested. Counts n and unique exclude missing values using the original column’s missingness rules, including tagged and SPSS user-missing values. List elements are counted without flattening: scalar missing elements are excluded, but NULL and empty elements remain observed identities. Matrix and nested data-frame columns count complete rows and omit rows containing any missing cell. Labels and units remain metadata; a zero-column selection returns an empty inventory.

browse() opens the selected data through tibble::view() interactively and returns those data invisibly. In a noninteractive script it returns the data without opening a viewer. It returns data, rather than a vector of column names; use ds() for names. Existing grouping follows s_select().

s_select() first tries dplyr::select() and uses dplyr::transmute() only when selection fails. A successful operation is no longer repeated, and its warnings are visible. A failed selection can still evaluate user code before fallback, so compute random draws and expressions with side effects in a prior mutate() step, then select the resulting column names.

Column summary statistics

summ() and tabstat() retain numeric and logical columns with no observed values, including zero-row inputs. They return n = 0, unique = 0, and NA for summary statistics, including sum. miss_n counts missing input rows. Zero-row grouped inputs do not create artificial groups.

Select statistics through .stat. The aliases missing, p25, p50, and p75 select miss_n, q1, median, and q3, respectively. Requested names and order are retained, and aliases can coexist with canonical names:

tidystata::summ(mtcars, mpg, .stat = c("missing", "miss_n", "p50", "median", "sum"))

Unknown statistics produce an error. sum is supported for numeric summaries; calendar dates, datetimes and hms times support neither sum nor skew/kurtosis.

When .type = "table" combines numeric and calendar summaries, shared location columns (such as mean) become character so the rows can coexist, with numeric values rounded to seven significant digits. Calendar spreads stay numeric, in days for Dates and seconds otherwise, and type records the unit ("date [days]"). Count columns remain numeric, and numeric-only summary tables retain numeric statistic columns. Default .type = "list" separates variable types and preserves numeric statistic types in the numeric summary.

With .keep_all = TRUE, character/list columns retain observed counts, missing counts and distinct observed values. Their numeric statistics are NA, even for numeric-looking text. The default .keep_all = FALSE removes these columns and errors if no supported columns remain. SPSS user-missing values and ranges are excluded before computing counts or numeric statistics. valid_pct is a fraction from zero to one, rather than a percentage from zero to 100.

An explicit .by overrides existing group_by() groups. A grouping key that collides with summary metadata is renamed with leading dots until unique among input names, with a message; input data remain unchanged. .missing = FALSE removes missing grouping keys only: numeric statistics always omit missing measured values. .name = FALSE drops the variable-name column only for one measured variable, including an empty grouped result.

List mode returns a single table for one type family, or named tables for mixed numeric, date, datetime and time (hms) families. Calendar locations are formatted text: Dates display calendar days, datetimes display their own time zone (the session zone when none is set) to minute precision, and times display hh:mm:ss. Calendar spreads (sd, se, mad, iqr) are difftime columns with one unit per column, days for Dates and otherwise the unit that fits the median spread, so they compare across rows and support arithmetic:

out <- summ(events, stamp, .by = site, .stat = c("mean", "sd"))
as.numeric(out$sd, units = "hours")

.duration_format is kept for compatibility but no longer changes the output.

Numeric calculations use double precision; converting large integer64 values can lose precision and emits a warning.

Factors use level codes with a warning; numeric labelled vectors use underlying values, excluding SPSS missing codes. Measured vectors and difftime retain original numeric units. SD is sample SD, quantiles use type 7, and MAD uses R’s default scaling. Skewness and excess kurtosis standardize central moments by sample SD; these are not claims of exact Stata equivalence. Undefined moments for singleton or constant data may be NA or NaN. See ?summ for details.

Cross-tabulation category names

tab2() and fre2() preserve categories matching the original variable names, n, or internal pivot names. A category matching the combined row-header name, or a literal "NA" alongside a missing column category, cannot be represented as unique output columns and produces a clear error.

The column category "total" is reserved for the marginal total in fre2(). Recode that category or use tab2() to avoid silently replacing category counts.

Measured vectors

var_type() identifies measured vectors as "units" in either abbreviation mode, including compound units such as m/s. var_unit() returns the unit string even for empty and all-missing measured vectors; ordinary vectors return NA_character_.

Historical problem repairs and explicit controls

Original PROBLEMS2.md notes are retained under .opencode/notes/; active regression tests preserve the repaired cases. A follow-up review changed four defaults to match the original requests: summ()/tabstat() sort groups like tab() (.sort = TRUE) and hide the name column for a single variable (.name = FALSE); timer() reports time on failure (on_error = TRUE); and xtile() follows Stata’s xtile rule. Pass .sort = FALSE, .name = TRUE or on_error = FALSE for the previous summary and timer behavior.

survey <- tibble::tibble(
  group = factor(c("high", "low", "low", NA), levels = c("low", "high")),
  x = c(10, 1, NA, NA), y = c(NA, 2, 4, NA)
)

# Groups are sorted by key; omission of summaries with no observed values is
# independent of removing rows with missing grouping keys (.missing = FALSE).
summ(survey, x, .by = group, .drop_empty = TRUE)
tabstat(survey, x, .stat = c("mean", "p2.5", "p97.5"))

# Larger .by blocks first; .desc still controls categories within each block.
tab(survey, x, .by = group, .group_order = "frequency", .desc = TRUE)

# Missingness controls are arguments, never extra data columns.
row_sum(survey[c("x", "y")], na.rm = FALSE)
row_mean(survey[c("x", "y")], na.rm = FALSE)
# Like pmin(): constants cap values and never fill all-missing rows.
survey |> dplyr::mutate(capped = row_min(x, 5))

# A named constant is computed; unnamed numbers remain column positions.
summ(survey, one = 1, .by = group)

tab(c(1, 1, 2)) # tibble with a value column and counts 2, 1
fre(c(1, 1, 2)) # tab1(), fre() and fre1() accept vectors too
ds(ds(survey), dplyr::starts_with("x"))

# Preserve the actual error while reporting elapsed time for failed work.
tryCatch(timer(stop("example failure"), on_error = TRUE), error = conditionMessage)

Summary percentiles use p0 through p100, including decimal percentages, and type-7 interpolation. q1 and q3 still mean the 25th and 75th percentiles. Requesting a small statistic set avoids unrelated calculations; it does not change their numerical definitions. All-missing summary rows remain by default.

Selections and computed expressions are classified before evaluation: tab(d, half = y / x) computes the ratio rather than selecting column y, and misspelled or out-of-range selections error with every unmatched name instead of evaluating an object of the same name. Use all_of() for name vectors.

For sf input, summary and frequency aggregation use nongeometry attributes: all sfc columns are excluded before selection and grouping. Results are ordinary tables. Geometry cannot be selected as a grouping or measured column for these operations. Selection, metadata inspection and browsing retain their existing spatial behavior.

Blank cross-tabulation column categories display as <empty>. When that synthetic header is already occupied, a numeric suffix distinguishes it without combining categories. Existing ambiguity errors described above still apply. Logical axes use FALSE, TRUE, then missing; other column categories follow factor levels or ascending values, with missing last. Stacked tables convert incompatible ordered factors, and labelled vectors with different labels, to character display values; list tables retain each variable’s class.

ds() can select names from a character inventory, including the result of an earlier ds() call. Inventory values must be unique, nonblank and nonmissing; an empty inventory is valid. Selection and renaming operate on those values, ignoring the vector’s own names. where() predicates require actual column data and are not available for a name inventory.

Some old notes describe convenience names rather than missing operations:

# Complete printing and interval browsing are explicit choices.
print_interval(survey, n = Inf, width = Inf)
browse(slice_interval(survey, n = 3))
preview_table(tab(survey, group)) # full data retained under a display policy

# Replace missing values after choosing the intended representation.
response <- haven::labelled(c(1, 2, NA), labels = c(Yes = 1, No = 2))
mvencode(response, 1) # retains numeric value labels
mvencode(haven::as_factor(response), "Yes") # factor replacement uses a level
haven::zap_missing(haven::labelled_spss(c(1, 99), na_values = 99))

tidyr::drop_na(survey, x)
unique(survey$group) # observed categories; levels() includes unused factor levels
list(first = 1, second = 2)[["second"]]

# Extract a fitted model separately so fitting errors retain their true cause.
fit <- stats::lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
# broom::tidy(fit)
# broom::glance(fit)
# Mixed models: broom.mixed::tidy(fit, effects = "fixed"); do not invent p-values.

# A direct lm coefficient display; the star here explicitly means p < .05.
coefficients <- stats::coef(summary(fit))
sprintf("%.3f%s (%.3f)", coefficients[, "Estimate"],
        ifelse(coefficients[, "Pr(>|t|)"] < .05, "*", ""),
        coefficients[, "Std. Error"])

# Numeric standardization uses sample SD and keeps missing positions missing.
measure <- c(1, 2, NA, 4)
stopifnot(stats::sd(measure, na.rm = TRUE) > 0)
standardized <- as.numeric(scale(measure))
# Constant/all-missing vectors need an explicit substantive policy before scaling.

# A model batch can share the same predictor specification.
models <- lapply(c("mpg", "disp"), function(response) {
  stats::lm(stats::reformulate(c("wt", "hp"), response), data = mtcars)
})

# Word output uses optional flextable directly.
# flextable::save_as_docx(flextable::flextable(as.data.frame(survey)),
#                       path = "survey.docx")

For count-table plots, use an explicit geom_col() rather than automatic distribution plots. Preserve date classes before selecting continuous date axes. For correlations, select the intended numeric columns and choose missingness explicitly in stats::cor(..., use = "pairwise.complete.obs"). Interval printing selects evenly spaced row positions; it does not estimate statistical quantiles.

New PCA, weighted-cut, regression, automatic plotting, profiling and output-preset APIs remain separate feature requests. The historical labelled-factor failure lacks its original call; representative replacement cases are tested, but do not prove that unspecified original case was reproduced.

Quantile bins and row summaries

xtile() follows Stata’s xtile rule with type-7 cutpoints: a value joins the first group whose cutpoint is at least that value. Equal values stay together and distinct values are never merged, so a 0/1 dummy gives two groups. Ties can leave fewer than n groups, numbered consecutively with a warning. Custom labels must match the effective group count. Empty, all-missing, constant, or invalid group-count inputs produce errors. Cutpoints are not promised to match Stata’s percentile definition exactly. Logical input is treated as 0/1, and labels = TRUE means the default interval labels. In a grouped data mask (group_by() |> mutate()), the default returns integer codes within each group, like Stata’s xtile, by(), because group-specific interval labels cannot be combined.

Use xtile(x, n = 10, method = "rank") when balanced counts matter more than keeping equal values together. Values sort ascending; original positions break ties. Equal values may enter different groups, and reordering tied rows can change their assignments. With k = min(n, observed_count), group sizes differ by at most one, with larger groups first. Missing positions remain missing. Requesting more groups than observed values warns and uses k; constant vectors are allowed in rank mode. Default labels are ordered "1" through "k", custom labels must have length k, and labels = FALSE returns integer group codes.

row_sum(..., na.rm = TRUE) keeps its existing missing-value omission default. Explicit FALSE makes any row containing an original missing value return NA. row_min() and row_max() accept .values alongside selected columns: one vector or a list of vectors, each of size one or the current row/group count. Scalar constants recycle without creating rows in empty inputs; supported types and original missingness are preserved. Bare numeric constants in ... are values, as in pmin(); select columns by position with c() or a helper. Constants never make an all-missing row observed.

Row helpers now use operation-specific output types. row_min() and row_max() preserve the compatible common input type: logical inputs return logical values and integer inputs return integers, replacing the earlier always-double extrema. Mixed logical/integer/double columns use their common numeric type. Supported ordered values also include character vectors (C lexical order, without parsing), ordered factors (level order), dates, date-times, durations, measured vectors, labelled vectors, and integer64. Compatible classes and metadata are retained, units are normalized, and labelled values are compared by their underlying values. Ordered factors cannot be mixed with non-ordered columns for extrema. Unordered factors, lists, complex values, and incompatible combinations are rejected for extrema.

Arithmetic on plain logical, integer, double, and numeric labelled columns returns doubles. Missingness is checked on the original values before stripping labels, including tagged and SPSS user-missing values. Columns from the same calendar family (Date or POSIXct) support class-preserving means and medians; convert explicitly before requesting calendar sums or dispersion. Durations support mean, median, sum, and standard deviation in a common difftime unit. Convert duration values explicitly to one numeric unit before variance. Compatible measured vectors on linear zero-origin scales normalize units before arithmetic; variance has squared units, while mean, median, sum, and standard deviation retain the common unit. Offset scales such as Celsius and Fahrenheit support means and medians only. Explicitly convert to a zero-origin unit before sums or dispersion. Nonlinear scales require explicit conversion to a linear unit before any arithmetic. Measured arithmetic requires units >= 1.0.0 and uses its public scale-conversion API. integer64 arithmetic requires explicit conversion, making any precision loss deliberate. Other incompatible arithmetic combinations produce an error.

For example, logical extrema retain their meaning and dates retain their class:

flags <- tibble::tibble(a = c(TRUE, FALSE, NA), b = c(FALSE, NA, NA))
tidystata::row_max(flags) # TRUE, FALSE, NA, with logical type

dates <- tibble::tibble(
  start = as.Date(c("2024-01-01", NA)),
  end = as.Date(c("2024-01-03", "2024-01-05"))
)
tidystata::row_min(dates)
tidystata::row_mean(dates)

row_unique() returns integer counts using compatible common types, preserving value identities rather than converting values to doubles. Compatible factors, calendar/measured vectors, labelled vectors, integer64, lists, and complex vectors are supported. List elements remain whole values. All missing values in a row count as one distinct category. row_miss() and row_non_miss() also return integers and use each original column’s is.na() result: scalar missing list elements are missing, while NULL and empty elements remain observed. For extrema and distinct counts, common-type conversion must preserve the original missingness of every value. Conflicting SPSS missing-value definitions that would turn an observed value into a missing value now produce an error; harmonize those definitions explicitly before combining the columns.

Arithmetic and extrema omit missing values. An all-missing row yields a typed NA, except row_sum() yields zero. row_var() and row_sd() use sample statistics and need at least two observed values. Every helper requires one-dimensional columns, rejects zero-column selections, and returns a typed empty vector for zero-row inputs. Inputs remain unchanged.

R 4.1.0 or later is required. Extrema, distinct counts, medians, and stable sample variance/standard deviation use native C++ kernels registered through cpp11. Means and sums retain base R compiled row aggregations. Rfast is no longer required.
